Lecture 6

Symmetry, projectors, and degeneracy

Symmetry shows, before the Hamiltonian is diagonalised, into which blocks its matrix splits and how many times, at least, its levels are degenerate. Characters give projectors that split a representation into its isotypic components. In a basis adapted to the symmetry, an operator that commutes with the group is block-diagonal, so each of its eigenvalues is at least as degenerate as the dimension of an irreducible representation. We apply this theorem to a particle hopping on a triangle, and in Lecture 7 to the vibrations of a molecule.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • Say when a group is a symmetry of a quantum system.
  • Project a representation onto its isotypic components, and build a symmetry-adapted basis.
  • Reduce an invariant operator to its matrices F(i)F^{(i)}F(i), and predict its degeneracies.

Symmetry in quantum mechanics

The state space of a quantum system is a complex vector space with an inner product, and a symmetry acts on it by a unitary representation. For a particle in space the states are wave functions, and the group acts by the function-space construction of Lecture 3, (ρ(g)ψ)(x⃗ )=ψ(g−1x⃗ ),\bigl(\rho(g)\psi\bigr)(\vec x\,)=\psi\bigl(g^{-1}\vec x\,\bigr),(ρ(g)ψ)(x)=ψ(g−1x), which is unitary for g∈O(3)g\in\Orth(3)g∈O(3): since ∣det⁡g∣=1\abs{\det g}=1∣detg∣=1, the substitution x⃗↦g−1x⃗\vec x\mapsto g^{-1}\vec xx↦g−1x preserves ∫∣ψ∣2\int\abs{\psi}^2∫∣ψ∣2. Physical models often restrict attention to a few states. The state space is then finite-dimensional; Example 6.3 below is one.

Definition 6.1 (Quantum symmetry). Let ρ\rhoρ be a unitary representation of a group GGG on the state space. Then GGG is a symmetry of the quantum system with Hamiltonian HHH if [ρ(g), H]=0for all g∈G.\bigl[\rho(g),\,H\bigr]=0 \qquad\text{for all }g\in G .[ρ(g),H]=0for all g∈G. In other words, HHH is an intertwiner of the representation ρ\rhoρ with itself (Lecture 3).

Proposition 6.2. If [ρ(g),H]=0[\rho(g),H]=0[ρ(g),H]=0 for all ggg, then every energy eigenspace {ψ:Hψ=λψ}\{\psi:H\psi=\lambda\psi\}{ψ:Hψ=λψ} is an invariant subspace. So each eigenspace carries a representation of GGG.

Proof. Hρ(g)ψ=ρ(g)Hψ=λ ρ(g)ψH\rho(g)\psi=\rho(g)H\psi=\lambda\,\rho(g)\psiHρ(g)ψ=ρ(g)Hψ=λρ(g)ψ. 

So the energy levels of a symmetric system are representations of its symmetry group. Which representations, and how large? Answering that is the business of this lecture. The answer needs only linearity: we shall apply the same theorem to the small-vibration model of Lecture 7.

Example 6.3 (A particle hopping on a triangle). Put one electron orbital on each of three identical atoms at the corners of an equilateral triangle — the three hydrogens of ammonia, or the three carbons of the cyclopropenyl ring — and write ∣j⟩\ket j∣j⟩ for the orbital on atom jjj (Figure 6.1). An orbital is a wave function centred on its atom, so a symmetry of the triangle carries the orbital on atom jjj to the orbital on the atom where jjj goes: ρ(g)∣j⟩=∣g(j)⟩\rho(g)\ket j=\ket{g(j)}ρ(g)∣j⟩=∣g(j)⟩, the permutation representation of Lecture 3. Keeping only these three orbitals, taken orthonormal, ⟨j|k⟩=δjk\braket{j}{k}=\delta_{jk}⟨j∣k⟩=δjk​, the state space is C3\C^3C3. The electron hops between neighbouring atoms with amplitude −t-t−t, where t>0t>0t>0, and on a triangle every two atoms are neighbours, so H=−t∑j≠k∣j⟩⟨k∣=−t (J−1)=−t(011101110),H=-t\sum_{j\neq k}\ket j\bra k=-t\,(J-\Id) =-t\begin{pmatrix}0&1&1\\1&0&1\\1&1&0\end{pmatrix},H=−tj=k∑​∣j⟩⟨k∣=−t(J−1)=−t​011​101​110​​, in the basis ∣1⟩,∣2⟩,∣3⟩\ket1,\ket2,\ket3∣1⟩,∣2⟩,∣3⟩, with JJJ the 3×33\times33×3 matrix of ones. The matrices of C3v≅S3C_{3v}\cong S_3C3v​≅S3​ are permutation matrices, and HHH commutes with every one of them, because each commutes with JJJ. So C3vC_{3v}C3v​ is a symmetry. The levels turn out to be −2t-2t−2t and a doubly degenerate ttt (Figure 6.1(b)). Why is ttt doubled, and can a symmetric change of HHH split it? The rest of the lecture answers both questions, and finds the eigenvectors without diagonalising HHH by hand.

Projection operators

Characters compute not only multiplicities: together with the operators ρ(g)\rho(g)ρ(g), they also find invariant subspaces. From here on GGG is finite and VVV is a finite-dimensional complex representation, and we keep two notations apart: superscripts in parentheses, V(i)V^{(i)}V(i), denote the abstract irreducible representations, and subscripts, ViV_iVi​, the pieces of a given representation VVV defined next.

Definition 6.4 (Isotypic components). Let (ρ,V)(\rho,V)(ρ,V) be a representation. The isotypic component ViV_iVi​ of type iii is the sum of all irreducible invariant subspaces of VVV equivalent to V(i)V^{(i)}V(i).

If V≅⨁imi V(i)V\cong\bigoplus_im_i\,V^{(i)}V≅⨁i​mi​V(i), the component ViV_iVi​ collects the mim_imi​ copies of V(i)V^{(i)}V(i), so dim⁡Vi=mini\dim V_i=m_in_idimVi​=mi​ni​ with ni=dim⁡V(i)n_i=\dim V^{(i)}ni​=dimV(i). When mi>1m_i>1mi​>1, the individual copies inside ViV_iVi​ are not unique, but the component is: the next theorem produces it from the character and the operators ρ(g)\rho(g)ρ(g), without choosing a decomposition.

The block-diagonalisation theorem

Let A∈Hom⁡G(V,V)A\in\Hom_G(V,V)A∈HomG​(V,V), that is, a linear operator on VVV that commutes with every ρ(g)\rho(g)ρ(g). Physically, AAA is a Hamiltonian, or the dynamical matrix of Lecture 7. Since each PiP_iPi​ is a combination of the ρ(g)\rho(g)ρ(g), Aρ(g)=ρ(g)A  for all g⟹APi=PiA⟹A Vi⊆Vi.A\rho(g)=\rho(g)A\ \text{ for all }g \quad\Longrightarrow\quad AP_i=P_iA \quad\Longrightarrow\quad A\,V_i\subseteq V_i .Aρ(g)=ρ(g)A  for all g⟹APi​=Pi​A⟹AVi​⊆Vi​. So AAA has no matrix elements between different components. What does it do inside one?

Here ν\nuν labels the basis vectors of each copy of V(i)V^{(i)}V(i), called its partners, and aaa counts the copies (Figure 6.2). For every aaa the vectors wν,aw_{\nu,a}wν,a​ transform by the same matrices D(i)(g)D^{(i)}(g)D(i)(g), the matrices of V(i)V^{(i)}V(i) in a basis fixed once; such copies are called aligned: ρ(g) wν,a=∑μDμν(i)(g) wμ,a.\rho(g)\,w_{\nu,a}=\sum_{\mu}D^{(i)}_{\mu\nu}(g)\,w_{\mu,a}.ρ(g)wν,a​=μ∑​Dμν(i)​(g)wμ,a​. Such a basis exists, and with an invariant inner product it can be chosen orthonormal. The D(i)(g)D^{(i)}(g)D(i)(g) are then unitary (Section 6.5).

Then (D(i)(g)⊗1mi)(eν⊗ea)=D(i)(g) eν⊗ea=∑μDμν(i)(g) eμ⊗ea,\bigl(D^{(i)}(g)\otimes\Id_{m_i}\bigr)(e_\nu\otimes e_a) =D^{(i)}(g)\,e_\nu\otimes e_a =\sum_\mu D^{(i)}_{\mu\nu}(g)\,e_\mu\otimes e_a ,(D(i)(g)⊗1mi​​)(eν​⊗ea​)=D(i)(g)eν​⊗ea​=μ∑​Dμν(i)​(g)eμ​⊗ea​, which is the transformation law: ρ(g)\rho(g)ρ(g) acts on ViV_iVi​ by D(i)(g)⊗1miD^{(i)}(g)\otimes\Id_{m_i}D(i)(g)⊗1mi​​.

Group theory fixes the blocks — their sizes mim_imi​, the multiplet sizes nin_ini​, the adapted basis — and the dynamics only fills in the small matrices F(i)F^{(i)}F(i), which the symmetry leaves free. An irreducible that occurs once needs no diagonalisation at all: its F(i)F^{(i)}F(i) is a number, and its adapted vectors are eigenvectors.

Corollary 6.8 (Symmetry-enforced degeneracy). For every number λ\lambdaλ, dim⁡ker⁡(A−λid⁡V)=∑ini dim⁡ker⁡(F(i)−λ1mi).\dim\ker(A-\lambda\id_V)=\sum_i n_i\,\dim\ker\bigl(F^{(i)}-\lambda\Id_{m_i}\bigr).dimker(A−λidV​)=i∑​ni​dimker(F(i)−λ1mi​​). So an eigenvalue with an eigenvector in ViV_iVi​ is at least nin_ini​-fold degenerate. If the eigenvalues of each reduced matrix are simple and no two reduced matrices share one, each eigenspace of AAA is exactly one irreducible multiplet.

Lecture 4 promised to tell a degeneracy that the symmetry enforces from an accidental one. Now we can. A degeneracy is

  • enforced if it is nin_ini​: every operator that commutes with GGG has it;

  • accidental if it is larger because an eigenvalue repeats inside one F(i)F^{(i)}F(i), or two reduced matrices share one, and no further symmetry explains it: a generic small perturbation that keeps all the symmetry removes it;

  • hidden if it is larger but enforced by a symmetry not yet taken into account: a larger group, or the reality of HHH (Section 6.5).

Degeneracy, further [self-study]

Schrödinger operators. For an unbounded HHH the commutator needs a domain. We assume that every ρ(g)\rho(g)ρ(g) maps the domain of HHH onto itself and that Hρ(g)ψ=ρ(g)HψH\rho(g)\psi=\rho(g)H\psiHρ(g)ψ=ρ(g)Hψ there. For a Schrödinger operator this asks more than an invariant potential: boundary conditions, if any, must be invariant too. The proposition below checks the commutator on smooth functions that vanish outside some ball, a domain that every ρ(g)\rho(g)ρ(g) preserves; that it then holds on the whole domain of HHH we take for granted.

Hence ∇2ρ(g)=ρ(g)∇2\nabla^2\rho(g)=\rho(g)\nabla^2∇2ρ(g)=ρ(g)∇2. The lower bound in infinite dimensions. The first half of Corollary 6.8 needs only Proposition 6.2, even on an infinite-dimensional state space. A finite-dimensional energy eigenspace and an isotypic component are both invariant, so their intersection is too. If it is not zero, it contains an irreducible invariant subspace of type iii, of dimension nin_ini​.

An orthonormal adapted basis exists. With an invariant inner product (Lecture 4), take the copies mutually orthogonal, choose an orthonormal basis of the first copy, and carry it to the other copies by unitary isomorphisms of representations. Schur’s lemma allows the latter: an isomorphism TTT between unitary irreducibles has T†T=c id⁡T^\dagger T=c\,\idT†T=cid with c>0c>0c>0, so T/cT/\sqrt cT/c​ is unitary.

But χ1\chi_1χ1​ and χ2\chi_2χ2​ are different representations of C3C_3C3​, and C3C_3C3​ alone does not force their energies to agree. What does?

The reflections of C3vC_{3v}C3v​ force it, and so, independently, does the reality of the Hamiltonian. First, the reflections reverse the direction round the triangle and swap the lines of v1v_1v1​ and v2v_2v2​, which together make up EEE. The mirror sss of Figure 6.1, for one, swaps ∣1⟩\ket1∣1⟩ and ∣2⟩\ket2∣2⟩ and fixes ∣3⟩\ket3∣3⟩: ρ(s)v1=ω2∣2⟩+ω∣1⟩+∣3⟩=v2.\rho(s)v_1=\omega^2\ket2+\omega\ket1+\ket3=v_2 .ρ(s)v1​=ω2∣2⟩+ω∣1⟩+∣3⟩=v2​. Since ρ(s)\rho(s)ρ(s) commutes with HHH, if v1v_1v1​ has energy λ\lambdaλ, then so does v2v_2v2​: Hv2=ρ(s)Hv1=λ ρ(s)v1=λ v2Hv_2=\rho(s)Hv_1=\lambda\,\rho(s)v_1=\lambda\,v_2Hv2​=ρ(s)Hv1​=λρ(s)v1​=λv2​. Second, the Hamiltonian is real: complex conjugation, which for a spinless particle is time reversal, commutes with HHH and turns v1v_1v1​ into v2v_2v2​, v1‾=ω2‾∣1⟩+ω‾∣2⟩+∣3⟩=ω∣1⟩+ω2∣2⟩+∣3⟩=v2,\overline{v_1}=\overline{\omega^2}\ket1+\overline{\omega}\ket2+\ket3 =\omega\ket1+\omega^2\ket2+\ket3=v_2 ,v1​​=ω2∣1⟩+ω∣2⟩+∣3⟩=ω∣1⟩+ω2∣2⟩+∣3⟩=v2​, so the two have the same energy. The second reason is general. For a Hamiltonian and representation matrices D(g)D(g)D(g) that are real in one basis, conjugation carries the isotypic component of an irreducible V(i)V^{(i)}V(i) to that of its conjugate V(i)‾\overline{V^{(i)}}V(i). Take as adapted basis of the second the conjugates of the adapted basis of the first. Then the reduced matrices obey F(iˉ)=F(i)‾F^{(\bar i)}=\overline{F^{(i)}}F(iˉ)=F(i), and since the eigenvalues of F(i)F^{(i)}F(i) are energies, hence real, the two blocks have the same eigenvalues. So irreducibles with non-real characters come in pairs with equal energies, and the pair forms one real multiplet. A degeneracy that looks accidental for the group at hand is often enforced by reality, or by a larger group.

Real, complex and quaternionic irreducibles. In the language of real types (Frobenius–Schur theory, stated without proof): an irreducible is of real type if it is equivalent to one by real matrices, of complex type if it is not equivalent to its conjugate, and of quaternionic type if it is equivalent to its conjugate but has no real form. The three cases are told apart by 1∣G∣∑gχ(g2)=1,0,−1\frac1{\abs G}\sum_g\chi(g^2)=1,0,-1∣G∣1​∑g​χ(g2)=1,0,−1. An irreducible of complex type must occur together with its conjugate in a real system, as χ1\chi_1χ1​ and χ2\chi_2χ2​ of C3C_3C3​ did on the triangle. The planar rotation representation of C3C_3C3​ shows the same thing for vibrations: a real matrix that commutes with the rotation R(2π/3)R(2\pi/3)R(2π/3) has the form a1+b R(π/2)a\Id+b\,R(\pi/2)a1+bR(π/2) with R(π/2)=(0−110)R(\pi/2)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)R(π/2)=(01​−10​), the quarter-turn; if it is also symmetric, then b=0b=0b=0, and so the two conjugate complex singlets form a real doublet.

Example 6.10 (The square well: forced and accidental degeneracy side by side). A particle in a two-dimensional infinite square well (x,y)∈[−a2,a2]2(x,y)\in[-\tfrac a2,\tfrac a2]^2(x,y)∈[−2a​,2a​]2 has the symmetry group D4D_4D4​ of the square. The eigenfunctions factorise: ψnm=φn(x)φm(y)\psi_{nm}=\varphi_n(x)\varphi_m(y)ψnm​=φn​(x)φm​(y) with Enm∝n2+m2E_{nm}\propto n^2+m^2Enm​∝n2+m2. Here φn\varphi_nφn​ is a cosine for odd nnn and a sine for even nnn, so that φn(−x)=(−1)n+1φn(x)\varphi_n(-x)=(-1)^{n+1}\varphi_n(x)φn​(−x)=(−1)n+1φn​(x).

Track the D4D_4D4​ action on the pair Wnm=span⁡{ψnm,ψmn}W_{nm}=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_{nm},\psi_{mn}\}Wnm​=span{ψnm​,ψmn​}, n≠mn\neq mn=m. The quarter-turn sends ψnm↦(−1)m+1ψmn\psi_{nm}\mapsto(-1)^{m+1}\psi_{mn}ψnm​↦(−1)m+1ψmn​, so its matrix is off-diagonal. The half-turn multiplies by (−1)n+m(-1)^{n+m}(−1)n+m. The axis reflections multiply by (−1)n+1(-1)^{n+1}(−1)n+1 and (−1)m+1(-1)^{m+1}(−1)m+1, and the diagonal reflection swaps the pair. The classes are (e, r2, 2r, 2σv, 2σd)(e,\,r^2,\,2r,\,2\sigma_v,\,2\sigma_d)(e,r2,2r,2σv​,2σd​): σv\sigma_vσv​ are the two axis reflections and σd\sigma_dσd​ the two diagonal ones (the classes of sss and rsrsrs in Lecture 5’s table of D4D_4D4​). The character of WnmW_{nm}Wnm​ is therefore χW=(2,  2(−1)n+m,  0,  (−1)n+1+(−1)m+1,  0).\chi_{W} =\bigl(2,\;2(-1)^{n+m},\;0,\;(-1)^{n+1}+(-1)^{m+1},\;0\bigr).χW​=(2,2(−1)n+m,0,(−1)n+1+(−1)m+1,0).

For n+mn+mn+m odd this is (2,−2,0,0,0)=χ5(2,-2,0,0,0)=\chi_5(2,−2,0,0,0)=χ5​, the two-dimensional irreducible representation of D4D_4D4​. So the degeneracy of, say, E12E_{12}E12​ is forced by symmetry. For n,mn,mn,m of equal parity the character is (2,2,0,±2,0)(2,2,0,\pm2,0)(2,2,0,±2,0). It decomposes into two inequivalent one-dimensional representations: the states ψnm±ψmn\psi_{nm}\pm\psi_{mn}ψnm​±ψmn​ belong to different symmetry types. Their shared energy, for instance E13=E31E_{13}=E_{31}E13​=E31​, is an accidental degeneracy of this special separable potential. A generic D4D_4D4​-symmetric perturbation of the well will split it. The well even harbours purely arithmetic accidents: E17=E55E_{17}=E_{55}E17​=E55​, from 1+49=25+251+49=25+251+49=25+25, connects different (n,m)(n,m)(n,m) pairs altogether. One simple system shows all three phenomena (Figure 6.4).

Hydrogen. The levels of the hydrogen atom are n2n^2n2-fold degenerate (ignoring spin), far more than the (2ℓ+1)(2\ell+1)(2ℓ+1)-fold multiplets of the rotation group. The extra degeneracy is enforced by a hidden four-dimensional rotation symmetry, generated by the angular momentum and the Runge–Lenz vector. A starred part of Lecture 13 touches on it.

Partner functions: aligning the copies. The character projector PiP_iPi​ picks out the isotypic component but does not see inside it. When the matrices D(i)D^{(i)}D(i) themselves are known, unitary, the operators Pμν(i)=ni∣G∣∑g∈GDμν(i)(g)‾  ρ(g)P^{(i)}_{\mu\nu} =\frac{n_i}{\abs G}\sum_{g\in G} \overline{D^{(i)}_{\mu\nu}(g)}\;\rho(g)Pμν(i)​=∣G∣ni​​g∈G∑​Dμν(i)​(g)​ρ(g) resolve ViV_iVi​ direction by direction. On a symmetry-adapted basis of any copy of V(i)V^{(i)}V(i) they act by Pμν(i) wβ,a=δνβ wμ,aP^{(i)}_{\mu\nu}\,w_{\beta,a}=\delta_{\nu\beta}\,w_{\mu,a}Pμν(i)​wβ,a​=δνβ​wμ,a​, and they annihilate the other types; the proof is one line from the great orthogonality theorem of Lecture 5’s self-study section. So Pμμ(i)P^{(i)}_{\mu\mu}Pμμ(i)​ projects onto the μ\muμth direction of each type-iii copy, and Pμν(i)P^{(i)}_{\mu\nu}Pμν(i)​ carries the ν\nuνth partner into the μ\muμth. Applied to a few trial vectors, they produce a whole symmetry-adapted basis, partners included, with the copies aligned as Section 6.3 requires.

Summary

  • Quantum symmetry. GGG is a symmetry when [ρ(g),H]=0[\rho(g),H]=0[ρ(g),H]=0 for every g∈Gg\in Gg∈G; then every energy eigenspace carries a representation of GGG (Definition 6.1, Proposition 6.2).
  • Projectors. Pi=ni∣G∣∑gχi(g)‾ρ(g)P_i=\frac{n_i}{\abs G}\sum_g\overline{\chi_i(g)}\rho(g)Pi​=∣G∣ni​​∑g​χi​(g)​ρ(g) projects onto the isotypic component ViV_iVi​; V=⨁iViV=\bigoplus_iV_iV=⨁i​Vi​, orthogonally when ρ\rhoρ is unitary, and the columns of PiP_iPi​ span ViV_iVi​ (Theorem 6.5).
  • Block diagonalisation. In an adapted basis, listed partner by partner, ρ(g)=D(i)(g)⊗1\rho(g)=D^{(i)}(g)\otimes\Idρ(g)=D(i)(g)⊗1 on ViV_iVi​, and an operator commuting with GGG acts by 1⊗F(i)\Id\otimes F^{(i)}1⊗F(i): nin_ini​ copies of an mi×mim_i\times m_imi​×mi​ matrix F(i)F^{(i)}F(i), with Fab(i)=⟨wν,a,A wν,b⟩F^{(i)}_{ab}=\inner{w_{\nu,a}}{A\,w_{\nu,b}}Fab(i)​=⟨wν,a​,Awν,b​⟩ in an orthonormal basis (Theorem 6.7). Group theory fixes the blocks, dynamics fills them in.
  • Degeneracy. dim⁡ker⁡(A−λid⁡V)=∑inidim⁡ker⁡(F(i)−λ1mi)\dim\ker(A-\lambda\id_V)=\sum_in_i\dim\ker(F^{(i)}-\lambda\Id_{m_i})dimker(A−λidV​)=∑i​ni​dimker(F(i)−λ1mi​​): a level of type iii is at least nin_ini​-fold degenerate, and generically exactly (Corollary 6.8); more is accidental, or hidden.
  • The triangle. The projectors give C3=L⊕V0\C^3=L\oplus V_0C3=L⊕V0​, of dimensions 111 and 222. In an orthonormal adapted basis the recipe gives F(A1)=−2tF^{(A_1)}=-2tF(A1​)=−2t and F(E)=tF^{(E)}=tF(E)=t, so H=diag⁡(−2t,t,t)H=\operatorname{diag}(-2t,t,t)H=diag(−2t,t,t) there: an enforced doublet at ttt. On two stacked triangles each irreducible occurs twice, and two 2×22\times22×2 reduced matrices give the singlets −2t+β±-2t+\beta_\pm−2t+β±​ and the doublets t+β±t+\beta_\pmt+β±​.

Self-check

10 questions. Answer without looking back at the notes.

1A potential UUU in the plane is unchanged by the rotations through ±2π/3\pm2\pi/3±2π/3 but by no reflection. Which group is a symmetry of H=−ℏ22m∇2+UH=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2+UH=−2mℏ2​∇2+U?

Here is the hint — try once more.The kinetic term commutes with every rotation and reflection. So which term decides?C3C_3C3​. The Laplacian commutes with every rotation and reflection, so GGG is a symmetry exactly when the potential is invariant, U(gx⃗)=U(x⃗)U(g\vec x)=U(\vec x)U(gx)=U(x) for all g∈Gg\in Gg∈G. The rotations through ±2π/3\pm2\pi/3±2π/3 leave UUU unchanged and no reflection does. That the kinetic term alone would allow more does not help: HHH commutes with ρ(g)\rho(g)ρ(g) only if both terms do.

2Let [ρ(g),H]=0[\rho(g),H]=0[ρ(g),H]=0 for all ggg. Why does each energy eigenspace carry a representation of GGG?

Here is the hint — try once more.Take an eigenvector ψ\psiψ with energy λ\lambdaλ, and apply HHH to ρ(g)ψ\rho(g)\psiρ(g)ψ.One line: Hρ(g)ψ=ρ(g)Hψ=λ ρ(g)ψH\rho(g)\psi=\rho(g)H\psi=\lambda\,\rho(g)\psiHρ(g)ψ=ρ(g)Hψ=λρ(g)ψ. So ρ(g)ψ\rho(g)\psiρ(g)ψ has the same energy, the eigenspace is an invariant subspace, and ρ\rhoρ restricted to it is a representation. Unitarity is not used. An eigenspace need not be irreducible: one that is not is an accidental degeneracy, or a sign of a larger symmetry.

3For a nonlinear classical system, a finite symmetry group only maps solutions to solutions. Why do quantum mechanics, and the small vibrations of Lecture 7, get far more out of it?

Here is the hint — try once more.What does the superposition principle make of the set of states?Linearity: superposition makes the states (or the small displacements) a vector space and the symmetry a linear representation on it. Then every energy level, or normal-mode frequency, is a representation, and its dimension is constrained by the irreducible ones. Noether's theorem needs a continuous family of symmetries, and a finite group stays finite.

4A representation of C3vC_{3v}C3v​ decomposes as V≅V(A1)⊕3V(E)V\cong V^{(A_1)}\oplus3V^{(E)}V≅V(A1​)⊕3V(E). What is tr⁡PE\tr P_EtrPE​?

PEP_EPE​ is the projection onto the isotypic component VEV_EVE​. What is the trace of a projection?

Here is the hint — try once more.666. The trace of a projection is the dimension of its image, and the image of PEP_EPE​ is VEV_EVE​, the three copies of EEE together: dim⁡VE=mEnE=3⋅2=6\dim V_E=m_En_E=3\cdot2=6dimVE​=mE​nE​=3⋅2=6. The lecture's projectors on C3\C^3C3 had the traces 1,0,21,0,21,0,2 in the same way.

5Let V≅2V(E)V\cong2V^{(E)}V≅2V(E) for C3vC_{3v}C3v​. What does the character of EEE determine inside VVV?

Here is the hint — try once more.On two stacked triangles, w2⊗e1, w3⊗e1w_2\otimes e_1,\,w_3\otimes e_1w2​⊗e1​,w3​⊗e1​ span one copy of EEE and w2⊗e2, w3⊗e2w_2\otimes e_2,\,w_3\otimes e_2w2​⊗e2​,w3​⊗e2​ another. Is there a third?PEP_EPE​ is built from the character, and its image is VEV_EVE​, the sum of all invariant subspaces equivalent to EEE: here all of VVV. The copies themselves are not determined. On the prism w2⊗e1, w3⊗e1w_2\otimes e_1,\,w_3\otimes e_1w2​⊗e1​,w3​⊗e1​ span one copy, w2⊗e2, w3⊗e2w_2\otimes e_2,\,w_3\otimes e_2w2​⊗e2​,w3​⊗e2​ a second, and w2⊗(11), w3⊗(11)w_2\otimes\binom11,\,w_3\otimes\binom11w2​⊗(11​),w3​⊗(11​) a third. The component is unique; its splitting into copies is a choice.

7An operator AAA commutes with every ρ(g)\rho(g)ρ(g). Why has it no matrix elements between different isotypic components?

Here is the hint — try once more.Compute APivAP_ivAPi​v for a vector vvv, using Aρ(g)=ρ(g)AA\rho(g)=\rho(g)AAρ(g)=ρ(g)A.APiv=PiAvAP_iv=P_iAvAPi​v=Pi​Av, because PiP_iPi​ is a sum of multiples of the ρ(g)\rho(g)ρ(g) and AAA commutes with each. So AAA maps the image of PiP_iPi​, which is ViV_iVi​, into itself. Nothing else is needed: AAA need not be Hermitian, nor preserve the inner product.

8An operator that commutes with C3vC_{3v}C3v​ acts on V≅3V(A1)⊕V(A2)⊕2V(E)V\cong3V^{(A_1)}\oplus V^{(A_2)}\oplus2V^{(E)}V≅3V(A1​)⊕V(A2​)⊕2V(E), of dimension 888. By the block-diagonalisation theorem, what is the size of the largest eigenvalue problem left to solve?

The reduced matrix F(i)F^{(i)}F(i) is mi×mim_i\times m_imi​×mi​, and it is solved once for all the partners.

Here is the hint — try once more.333. The reduced matrices are 3×33\times33×3 for A1A_1A1​, 1×11\times11×1 for A2A_2A2​ and 2×22\times22×2 for EEE, the last solved once for both partners. The 8×88\times88×8 problem becomes problems of sizes 333, 111 and 222. The size is the multiplicity mim_imi​, not the dimension nin_ini​ and not minim_in_imi​ni​.

9A Hamiltonian with symmetry C3vC_{3v}C3v​ has a fourfold level. A small perturbation that keeps C3vC_{3v}C3v​ splits it into two doublets. Was the fourfold degeneracy enforced?

Here is the hint — try once more.The enforced degeneracy of a level of type iii is nin_ini​. What are the dimensions of the irreducible representations of C3vC_{3v}C3v​?No. The irreducibles of C3vC_{3v}C3v​ have dimensions 1,1,21,1,21,1,2. A fourfold level of type EEE is an eigenvalue repeated inside the reduced matrix F(E)F^{(E)}F(E), which is accidental unless a larger symmetry enforces it. The stacked triangles show one: at t′=0t'=0t′=0 the layers decouple and F(E)=t 1F^{(E)}=t\,\IdF(E)=t1, and any t′≠0t'\neq0t′=0 splits the level into the doublets t∓t′t\mp t't∓t′.

10A real Hamiltonian HHH commutes with a group GGG acting by real matrices, and an irreducible V(i)V^{(i)}V(i) of GGG has a character that is not real. What can you say about the energy levels of type iii?

Here is the hint — try once more.Complex conjugation commutes with a real HHH and real matrices D(g)D(g)D(g). Where does it send the isotypic component of V(i)V^{(i)}V(i)?Conjugation carries the isotypic component of V(i)V^{(i)}V(i) to that of its conjugate V(i)‾\overline{V^{(i)}}V(i), which is a different irreducible because χi\chi_iχi​ is not real, and the reduced matrices obey F(iˉ)=F(i)‾F^{(\bar i)}=\overline{F^{(i)}}F(iˉ)=F(i); a Hermitian FFF has real eigenvalues, so the two blocks have the same ones. The pair forms one real multiplet of size 2ni2n_i2ni​, more than GGG alone enforces. On the triangle, χ1\chi_1χ1​ and χ2\chi_2χ2​ of C3C_3C3​ pair into the doublet EEE.
